Where We Are

Recap: MongoDB in One Slide

db.inventory.find(
    { tags: "red" },           // WHERE
    { _id: 0, instock: 0 } )   // SELECT
  .sort( { "dim.0": -1 } )     // ORDER BY
  .limit(2)                    // LIMIT
db.zips.aggregate( [
  { $group: { _id: "$state", totalPop: { $sum: "$pop" } } },
  { $match: { totalPop: { $gte: 200000 } } },
  { $sort:  { totalPop: -1 } }
] )   // GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY as stages
Document store: input = collections, output = collections. Retrieval is find, aggregation is a pipeline of stages in the order you write.

Beyond One Collection

  • Data models:
    • Key-value
    • JSON
  • We queried one MongoDB collection at a time
  • Now: parallel batch processing over many machines

Why Distribute Batch Work

  • Relational databases can also execute queries in parallel
  • Large batch jobs may need custom record-processing functions
  • MapReduce is a distributed programming model for such computation
  • First, let’s study how data is stored in such systems

Distributed File System (DFS)

  • For very large files: TBs, PBs
  • Each file is partitioned into chunks, 64 MB in the original GFS design
  • Replication factor and rack placement are configured for fault tolerance
  • Implementations:
    • Google’s DFS: GFS, proprietary
    • Hadoop’s DFS: HDFS, open source

MapReduce

  • Google: paper published 2004
  • Free variant: Hadoop
  • MapReduce: high-level programming model and implementation for large-scale parallel data processing

Case study: Google's Web IndexGoogle rewrote its production indexing system for web search on MapReduce

> 20 TBraw crawled documents, input to the indexer
5 to 10MapReduce jobs in a row build the index
3,800 → 700lines of C++ for one indexing phase
MapReduce moved distribution and recovery code out of the indexing application

Typical Problems Solved by MapReduce

  • Read a lot of data
  • Map: extract something you care about from each record
  • Shuffle and Sort
  • Reduce: aggregate, summarize, filter, transform
  • Write the results
Paradigm stays the same,
change map and reduce functions for different problems

Data Model

Files!
A file = a bag of (key, value) pairs
  • A MapReduce program:
    • Input: a bag of (inputkey, value) pairs
    • Output: a bag of (outputkey, value) pairs
      • outputkey is optional

Step 1: the MAP Phase

User provides the MAP-function:
  • Input: (input key, value)
  • Output: bag of (intermediate key, value)
System applies the map function in parallel to all (input key, value) pairs in the input file

Step 2: the SHUFFLE Phase

This is completely internal to the system
  • Input: Pairs of (intermediate key, value)
  • Output: Pairs of (intermediate key, bag of values with the same intermediate key)
I.e., group all values with the same key

Step 3: the REDUCE Phase

User provides the REDUCE function:
  • Input: (intermediate key, bag of values)
  • Output: bag of output (values)
System groups all pairs with the same intermediate key, and passes the bag of values to the REDUCE function

Example

  • Counting the number of occurrences of each word in a large collection of documents
  • Each Document
    • The key = document id (did)
    • The value = set of words (word)
map(String key, String value):
  // key: document name
  // value: document contents
  for each word w in value:
    emitIntermediate(w, "1");
reduce(String key, Iterator values):
  // key: a word
  // values: a list of counts
  int result = 0;
  for each v in values:
    result += ParseInt(v);
  emit(AsString(result));

Example: The Data Flow

Map emits pairs, shuffle groups them by key, reduce folds each group

Workers

  • A worker is a process that executes one task at a time
  • This simplified model uses one task slot per worker; real runtimes configure concurrency

Map Tasks and Reduce Tasks

M map tasks and R reduce tasks, usually many more than there are workers

Fault Tolerance

  • With independent server failures averaging one per year, 10,000 servers see a failure about every 53 minutes on average
  • MapReduce handles fault tolerance by writing intermediate files to disk:
    • Mappers write file to local disk
    • Lost map output is recomputed; failed reduce tasks restart on another worker

Demo: MapReduce Word CountReducer load is measured by input-value count, not elapsed time

  1. Vary R from 1 to 4 and watch the largest load
  2. Turn on the hot key and vary R again

Answer: MapReduce Word CountA hot key creates a load floor that additional reducers cannot remove

Hashing sends all values of one key to one reducer, so the reducer with alarm reads at least 24 values for any R
With the hot key, R = 4 carries more load than R = 3

Caveat: Data SkewOne hot key makes one task the bottleneck while the others sit idle

Remedy: for counts, salt the hot key, count the parts, then sum the partial counts
Salting divides the hot key into partial counts before a final merge

MapReduce Summary

  • MapReduce offers a simple abstraction, and handles distribution + fault tolerance
  • Speedup from dynamically allocating map and reduce tasks and to servers. Skew is possible!
  • Write intermediate results to disk for fault tolerance but can be slow

Issues with MapReduce

  • Difficult to write more complex queries
    • Everything has to be expressed as map-reduce
  • Need multiple MapReduce jobs: dramatically slows down because it writes all (intermediate) results to disk

Spark APIs

One core, four libraries, one DataFrame API on top

Driver and Executors

Driver plans, cluster manager hands out, executors run and hold the blocks

Why Spark? – Programmability

WordCount in 50+ lines of Java MR
public class WordCount {
  public static class TokenizerMapper
      extends Mapper<Object, Text, Text, IntWritable> { ... }
  public static class IntSumReducer
      extends Reducer<Text, IntWritable, Text, IntWritable> { ... }
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    Job job = Job.getInstance(conf, "word count");
    job.setMapperClass(TokenizerMapper.class); ...
  }
}
WordCount in 3 lines of Spark
val f = sc.textFile(inputPath)
val w = f.flatMap(l => l.split(" ")).map(word => (word, 1)).cache()
w.reduceByKey(_ + _).saveAsTextFile(outputPath)

RDDs: Partitions and Lineage

  • RDD = Resilient Distributed Datasets
    • A partitioned, immutable collection with lineage
    • Lineage: expression that says how that relation was computed (e.g., a relational algebra plan)
  • Transformations return RDDs; actions return values or write output
  • If an executor loses partitions, the driver uses lineage to recompute them from available ancestors or source data

RDD Lineage

Each RDD remembers the function that made it from its parent

MapReduce vs RDD

Hadoop MapReduce: materialize between jobs
Spark: pipeline transformations and optionally cache reused data
Hadoop:
Map -> local disk -> shuffle -> Reduce -> HDFS -> next job
Spark:
rdd.map(...).filter(...).groupBy(...).collect()
→ Spark builds a DAG internally; shuffles and spills can still use disk.

RDD Execution Process

Code → DAG → stages → tasks → workers

Lazy Transformations and Actions

  • A Spark program consists of:
    • Transformations (map, reduceByKey, join…). Lazy
    • Actions (count, reduce, save...). Eager
  • Eager: operators are executed immediately
  • Lazy: operators are not executed immediately
    • A operator tree is constructed in memory instead
    • Similar to a relational algebra tree

RDD Transformations

Transformations go from RDD to RDD; nothing has run yet

RDD Actions

An action turns the tree into a value; that is when work happens

RDD Programming – Persistence (a.k.a. Cache)

errors = sc.textFile("logs/").filter(
    lambda line: line.startswith("ERROR")).persist()

errors.count()  # first action computes and caches
errors.filter(lambda line: "sqlite" in line).count()
  • Cached partitions can serve later actions
  • Lost or evicted partitions are recomputed from available ancestors
  • Caching is not a durable backup
persist() enables reuse; lineage enables recomputation

RDD Programming – Example

R(A,B) S(A,C)
SELECT count(*) FROM R, S
WHERE  R.B > 200 AND S.C < 100 AND R.A = S.A
def pair(line):
    a, value = line.split(",")
    return int(a), int(value)
R = sc.textFile("R.csv").map(pair)
S = sc.textFile("S.csv").map(pair)
Parse headerless CSV lines into (key, value) pairs; join uses the first element as the key.

DataFrame Abstraction

Distributed collection of data grouped into named columns (i.e. RDD with schema)
  • DSL designed for common tasks
    • Metadata
    • Sampling
    • Project, filter, aggregation, join, …
    • UDFs
Available in Python, Scala, Java, and R (via SparkR)

DataFrame Operations

DataFrames hold rows with a known schema and offer relational operations on them through a DSL
val users = spark.sql("select * from users")
val massUsers = users('country === "Canada")   // expression AST, not a closure
massUsers.count()
massUsers.groupBy("name").avg("age")
'country === "Canada" builds an expression tree Spark can read; a lambda in filter is opaque to the engine.

The Optimized Plan

SQL and DataFrames meet in a logical plan; the optimizer is back

RDD vs DataFrame

AspectRDDDataFrame
LevelLow-level API (manual control)High-level API (table abstraction)
OptimizationNo SQL expression optimizerCatalyst optimizer (automatic)
ExecutionUser functions over objectsOptimized SQL expressions and generated code
SchemaUnstructuredSchema-aware
Ease of useComplex functional codeSimple SQL-like syntax
When to useCustom logic, unstructured dataETL, analytics, ML pipelines

pySpark

  • We are using the Python programming interface to Spark (pySpark)
  • pySpark provides an easy-to-use programming abstraction and parallel runtime:
    • “Here’s an operation, run it on all of the data”
  • spark.apache.org/docs/latest/programming-guide.html
  • spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/index.html

pySpark – Spark Driver and Workers

  • A Spark program is two programs:
    • A driver program and a workers program
  • Worker programs run on cluster nodes or in local threads
  • RDDs are distributed across workers

pySpark – Creating RDDs

Create RDDs from Python collections (lists)
>>> data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
>>> data
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

>>> rDD = sc.parallelize(data, 4)
>>> rDD
ParallelCollectionRDD[0] at parallelize at PythonRDD.scala:229
sc.parallelize() creates a four-partition RDD; transformations wait for an action

Map and Filter in PySpark

>>> rdd = sc.parallelize([1, 2, 3, 4])
>>> rdd.map(lambda x: x * 2).collect()
[2, 4, 6, 8]

>>> rdd.filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0).collect()
[2, 4]

>>> rdd2 = sc.parallelize([1, 4, 2, 2, 3])
>>> sorted(rdd2.distinct().collect())
[1, 2, 3, 4]
Function literals (lambdas) are closures automatically passed to workers

Key Aggregation in PySpark

>>> rdd = sc.parallelize([(1,2), (3,4), (3,6)])
>>> sorted(rdd.reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b).collect())
[(1, 2), (3, 10)]

>>> rdd2 = sc.parallelize([(1,'a'), (2,'c'), (1,'b')])
>>> rdd2.sortByKey().keys().collect()
[1, 1, 2]

pySpark – RDD Actions

>>> rdd = sc.parallelize([1, 2, 3])
>>> rdd.reduce(lambda a, b: a * b)
Value: 6

>>> rdd.take(2)
Value: [1,2] # as list

>>> rdd.collect()
Value: [1,2,3] # as list

DataFrames and pandas

# Small results only: collect to the driver
pandas_df = spark_df.toPandas()

# Create a Spark DataFrame from Pandas
spark_df = spark.createDataFrame(pandas_df)

DataFrame Joins

  • SparkSQL and Spark DataFrames join() supports:
    • inner, outer, left outer, right outer, semijoin
  • For Pair RDDs, pySpark supports:
    • inner join(), leftOuterJoin(), rightOuterJoin(), fullOuterJoin()

Shuffle Join

Reshuffle both sides on the join key, then each server joins locally

Shuffle Join by Key

Tag each tuple with its source; the reduce pairs R with S inside one key

Broadcast Join

Broadcast the small table; the large input can keep its existing partitions

Broadcast Join in Each Worker

A hash table of S in every mapper; no shuffle, no reduce

Comparison of Join Algorithms

Partitioned Hash JoinBroadcast Join
When to useBoth tables are large, or not already partitioned by the join keyOne table is very small (MBs to tens of MBs) and can be replicated to all workers
Data scaleLarge ↔ Large (fact–fact join)Large ↔ Small (fact–dimension join)
Data movementBoth tables are shuffled across the networkOnly the small table is sent to all nodes
PerformanceShuffle cost depends on size, partitioning and skewAvoids shuffling the large input; broadcast and memory costs remain
LimitationsHigh shuffle cost, longer execution timeSmall-table size limit, risk of out-of-memory
Rule of thumbIf both are big, partitionIf one is small, broadcast

Spark SQL: One Query, Two Ways

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

sales = spark.read.parquet("sales/")
(sales.filter(sales.region == "Asia")
      .groupBy("product")
      .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"))
      .orderBy(F.desc("total")))
sales.createOrReplaceTempView("sales")
spark.sql("""
  SELECT product, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM sales WHERE region = 'Asia'
  GROUP BY product ORDER BY total DESC""")
Both go through the same optimizer and run as the same plan

Files In, Files Out

events = (spark.read
          .option("header", True)
          .option("inferSchema", True)
          .csv("raw/events/*.csv"))

daily = events.groupBy("date", "machine").count()

(daily.write
       .mode("overwrite")
       .partitionBy("date")
       .parquet("clean/daily_counts/"))
Read raw files, transform, write Parquet; the write is the action that runs it all

Where Spark Runs

WhereExamplesUse it when
Your laptoppip install pyspark, master local[*]learning, testing on a sample
Managed platformDatabricks, AWS EMR, Google Dataprocthe data does not fit on one machine
Not Spark at allpandas, Polars, DuckDBthe data fits on one machine
If the data fits on one machine, you do not need Spark

Takeaway: Big Data I

1When data outgrows one machine, map → shuffle → reduce divides the work; a hot key can still leave one slow task
2Spark uses lineage to recover lost partitions and can cache reused data
3Write DataFrames or SQL; an action runs the lazy plan, and joins often pay for shuffles
